byTheNumbers.title: The year in numbers
byTheNumbers.standfirst: Nine in every hundred Americans were online and one in eight had a mobile phone, as the web went commercial.

items.title: Population
items.summary: The United States had about 266 to 268 million people in 1995.

sources.label: World Bank, World Development Indicators: Population, total
Our World in Data: Population (UN World Population Prospects, HYDE)

items.title: Life expectancy at birth
items.summary: A baby born in 1995 could expect to live about 75.6 years.

sources.label: World Bank, World Development Indicators: Life expectancy at birth, total (years)
Our World in Data: Life expectancy (UN World Population Prospects and other series)

items.title: Online
items.summary: About 9 percent of Americans used the internet in 1995.

sources.label: World Bank, World Development Indicators: Individuals using the Internet (% of population)

items.title: Mobile phones
items.summary: There were about 13 mobile subscriptions for every 100 people.

sources.label: World Bank, World Development Indicators: Mobile cellular subscriptions (per 100 people)

items.title: Infant deaths
items.summary: About 8 of every 1,000 babies died before their first birthday.

sources.label: World Bank, World Development Indicators: Mortality rate, infant (per 1,000 live births)

items.title: Motor vehicles
items.summary: Registrations reached 201.5 million: 128.4 million cars, 72.5 million trucks (including pickups and vans) and 686,000 buses.

sources.label: Historical Statistics of the United States, Table Df339-342: Motor vehicle registrations
FHWA Highway Statistics Summary to 1995, Table MV-200: Motor vehicle registrations

byTheNumbers.scarcityNote: Literacy and household size were not found for 1995. There was no census; population figures are mid-year estimates.

foodAndKitchen.title: Food and the kitchen
foodAndKitchen.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced 1995 food prices, appliance counts or meals.

clothingAndStyle.title: What people wore
clothingAndStyle.standfirst: Flannel shirts and baggy jeans gave way to slip dresses and baby tees, and sportswear went out in public.

items.title: Grunge fades
items.summary: Grunge dress, which peaked in late 1993 and early 1994, rapidly declined in 1994 as fashion became more feminine and form-fitting; flannel shirts stayed popular from 1991 to 1997.

sources.label: Wikipedia: 1990s in Western fashion

items.title: The slip dress
items.summary: Slip dresses first became widely worn in the mid-1990s, and in 1994 the commonest young women's look was a short black slip dress over a tight white T-shirt.

sources.label: Wikipedia: 1990s in Western fashion

items.title: Baby tees and tartan
items.summary: In 1994-95 the 'school girl' look included baby doll tees, tartan minikilts and knee-high socks.

sources.label: Wikipedia: 1990s in Western fashion

items.title: Leggings and sneakers
items.summary: In 1994 loungewear for young women was typically black Lycra leggings or bike shorts, large T-shirts, sweatshirts and athletic sneakers, and sportswear became acceptable in public over the mid- to late 1990s.

sources.label: Wikipedia: 1990s in Western fashion

items.title: Men's clothes
items.summary: From 1995 men wore overalls, straight-leg jeans, plaid pants and flat-front chinos, and black or neon high-top sneakers replaced combat boots in a mid-1990s trend list.

sources.label: Wikipedia: 1990s in Western fashion

items.title: Navel piercing
items.summary: Tattoos and body piercing beyond the ears became mainstream in the 1990s, and navel piercings were gaining popularity around the mid-1990s.

sources.label: Wikipedia: 1990s in Western fashion

workAndWages.title: Work and wages
workAndWages.standfirst: A production worker in manufacturing earned about $514 a week.

items.title: A manufacturing paycheque
items.summary: A production worker in manufacturing earned $12.37 an hour, or $514.49 a week, on average; in durable goods $548.23 and in non-durable goods $468.99.

sources.label: Historical Statistics of the United States, Table Ba4361-4366: Hourly and weekly earnings of production workers in manufacturing, 1909-1995

workAndWages.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced figures for 1995 hours, women's work or the minimum wage.

schoolAndChildhood.standfirst: A third of public schools were connected to the internet, and half within a year.

spotlight.title: Getting online
spotlight.standfirst: In 1995 the internet's backbone went commercial, Windows 95 put a dial-up connection in the box, and about 9 percent of Americans were online.

items.title: The backbone goes commercial
items.summary: The optical backbone of the NSFNET was decommissioned in 1995, removing the last restrictions on commercial traffic, and its traffic was handed to commercial providers including MCI, PSINet and Sprint.

sources.label: Wikipedia: History of the Internet

items.title: Windows 95
items.summary: Windows 95 went on sale on 24 August 1995; it shipped with Dial-Up Networking and the Microsoft Network but without Internet Explorer, which came in the Plus! pack, and one million copies shipped worldwide in four days.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Windows 95

items.title: Amazon opens its shop
items.summary: Amazon's website launched on 16 July 1995, initially selling books sourced from wholesalers and publishers.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Amazon (company)

items.title: Schools online
items.summary: Internet access in public schools rose from 35 percent in fall 1994 to 50 percent in 1995, but only 8 percent of instructional rooms were connected in 1995, up from 3 percent.

sources.label: NCES: Internet Access in Public Schools and Classrooms, 1994-98
NCES: Indicator of the Month, Internet Access in Public and Private Schools

items.title: Computers at home
items.summary: 22.8 percent of households had a computer in 1993 and 36.6 percent in October 1997; the Census Bureau did not ask in 1995.

sources.label: U.S. Census Bureau: Computer use and ownership (Current Population Survey, 1993 and 1997)
